Coburg
KOH-burg
n. (the Franconian fortress where Luther waited out the Diet of Augsburg in 1530)
German Coburg, perhaps the fortress of the cow pasture or of a personal name, with Burg, a castle.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Coburg in Franconia, the southernmost point of Electoral Saxony, has above it the Veste Coburg, one of the largest fortresses in Germany. Luther was still an outlaw under the Edict of Worms and could not safely go to Augsburg for the Diet of 1530, so he was left at Coburg, the nearest Saxon ground, while Melanchthon presented the Confession. He stayed from April to October with Veit Dietrich as his companion, worked on the Psalms and the Prophets, wrote a stream of letters urging Melanchthon to stop being afraid, learned at Coburg of his father's death, and preached to the household. He wrote to Melanchthon that he was tired of their anxiety, which was unbelief rather than prudence. The dictionary records Coburg for those six months, which are a study in waiting while other men act. Scripture has words for it: be not afraid of their faces, for I am with thee to deliver thee; and they shall fight against thee, but they shall not prevail against thee.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines afraid as struck with fear; to deliver as to free and rescue; to prevail as to overcome; a face as the front of the head and presence; and anxiety as painful uneasiness of mind.

expand to see more

AFRAID, a. Impressed with fear or apprehension; fearful; struck with fear; terrified.

DELIVER, v.t. To free; to release, as from restraint; to set at liberty; to rescue from danger or evil.

PREVAIL, v.i. To overcome; to gain the victory or superiority; to be in force; to have effect.

FACE, n. The front part of an animal's head; the surface of a thing; presence; appearance; look.

ANXIETY, n. Concern or solicitude respecting some event, future or uncertain, which disturbs the mind.

Key Scripture

Jer 1:8 — "Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee, saith the LORD."

Jer 1:19 — "And they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee; for I am with thee, saith the LORD, to deliver thee."

Psa 91:2 — "I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust."

Isa 32:17 — "And the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever."

Modern Corruption

Franconian fortress where Luther, still an outlaw, spent April to October 1530 while Melanchthon presented the Confession at Augsburg.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Luther kept writing down the road to Augsburg, that fear of men is answered by a promise of presence and not by a calculation of odds. God's word to a young prophet is the text for it: “Be not afraid of their faces: for I am with thee to deliver thee, saith the LORD” (Jer 1:8), followed by a forecast that concedes the attack and denies the outcome, “they shall fight against thee; but they shall not prevail against thee” (Jer 1:19).

The live temptation is to call anxiety prudence, which is precisely the charge Luther laid against Melanchthon in those letters. The Psalmist's confession names an object instead of a probability: “I will say of the LORD, He is my refuge and my fortress: my God; in him will I trust” (Psa 91:2). And Isaiah describes the by-product of doing right rather than of winning: “the work of righteousness shall be peace; and the effect of righteousness quietness and assurance for ever” (Isa 32:17). Luther spent six months in a castle he could not leave, translating the Prophets.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew yarea (H3372), to fear; Hebrew natsal (H5337), to deliver; Hebrew yakol (H3201), to prevail; Hebrew betach (H0983), security.

expand to see more

Hebrew yarea (H3372) — to fear, to be afraid; “Be not afraid of their faces”, Jeremiah 1:8.

Hebrew natsal (H5337) — to snatch away, to deliver; “for I am with thee to deliver thee”, Jeremiah 1:8.

Hebrew yakol (H3201) — to be able, to prevail; “but they shall not prevail against thee”, Jeremiah 1:19.

Hebrew metsudah (H4686) — a stronghold, a fortress; “He is my refuge and my fortress”, Psalm 91:2.

Hebrew betach (H0983) — security, confidence; “quietness and assurance for ever”, Isaiah 32:17.

Usage

"“Be not afraid of their faces” (Jer 1:8) — the text for six months of waiting."

"“they shall not prevail against thee” (Jer 1:19) — the attack conceded, the outcome denied."

"“the work of righteousness shall be peace” (Isa 32:17) — a by-product of doing right."
